title: How much e-waste still comes into Thailand?

voiceover.text: Thailand banned electronic waste imports in twenty twenty. So how much still comes in, through customs?
We looked at U.N. Comtrade: the U.N. trade database, built from each country's customs records.
For years, there was almost nothing: a few tonnes of battery waste a year.
In twenty sixteen, a military government order exempted some factories, including waste plants, from town-planning rules. By twenty nineteen: four hundred tonnes a year.
In September twenty twenty, the import ban took effect. That year: about two hundred forty tonnes, from just five countries.
The next year: three hundred thirty-five.
From twenty twenty-two, the customs codes got more detailed, so we can see every kind of e-waste.
And twenty twenty-five was the biggest year on record: over twelve hundred tonnes.
But the value fell, from seven million dollars to one and a half. More waste, less money.
The top sender keeps changing. The U.S. in twenty eighteen. Then Japan. South Korea through the ban years. Then Japan again: seven hundred tonnes, almost all battery waste.
Then in twenty twenty-five, the U.S. came back, with eleven hundred tonnes.
That's about nine in every ten tonnes, mostly general e-waste and scrap for precious metals.
In the ban year, only five countries sent battery waste. By twenty twenty-five, it was thirteen. Count every kind of e-waste, and it's twenty-three.
Over twelve hundred tonnes a year, declared at customs. Where does it all end up?
We found this on Querious, in customs data from U.N. Comtrade.
Group by country, press Run, and see who sends the most.
Or connect Querious to your own A.I. and tools, and just ask.
The data is open. The question is yours.
